properties.name: The graph answers "as of epoch n" itself — a design's own time axis is not a git lookup
properties.statement:
A user must be able to ask the design a temporal question and get an answer, without going to git, without knowing a ref, and without anyone having rendered a document first. "What capabilities are due to be released in epoch 5?" and "what didn't we achieve that we were supposed to in increment 10?" — Anthony's own two questions, 2026-07-30 — are the acceptance test.

REWORDED 2026-07-30 ON ANTHONY'S WORD, and the change is substantive rather than editorial, so the original is preserved at `snap:epoch:planning-axis-intent:req:graph-indexes-snapshots`. This requirement was first written as an INDEX: "the graph tracks its own snapshots — which epoch_n or increment_n a thing belongs to, and WHERE THAT SNAPSHOT LIVES (the git ref)". That framing assumed the snapshot was a thing sitting in git that the graph pointed at. It is not, and the intent behind the original sentence is better served without it.

WHY THE INDEX FRAMING WENT. His stated intent never changed: "a user shouldn't have to remember which git branch a particular epoch or increment is in." Storing plan slices in git and indexing them satisfies the letter of that. Storing nothing in git satisfies it absolutely — there are no branches to remember because nothing was put in one. His words on 2026-07-30: "we could do this completely in the graph without git. We are just using git as a means to render a snapshot in time… let the agent/user figure out how to render the snapshot."

WHAT THIS REQUIRES, and it is a query surface rather than a file format. The graph must be able to answer, for any epoch or increment: what is scheduled to be satisfied by it; what was actually satisfied when it arrived; and the delta between those. The temporal machinery to do this already exists in part — epochs, Snapshots that capture a node's incoming and outgoing edges, and `compare_designs` — so this is largely a matter of reading what is already recorded rather than recording something new.

WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT MATERIALISED. No per-epoch branch, no per-epoch file, no rendered roadmap held as a record. Every materialised artifact acquires a staleness problem the moment the graph moves, and reflow2 has three live examples of paying that cost (`docs/design/reflow2.json`'s gate, `dataflow.html`'s check, and `docs/loop-model.json`, which became permanently unreproducible on 2026-07-30). Not materialising is the only way to have no drift. Rendering stays an OUTPUT — `render_views.py` may emit an epoch view whenever a person wants one, as a disposable projection, never as the record.

THE INFORMATION IS STILL IN GIT, WHICH IS WHY NOTHING IS LOST. The schedule lives in the graph, the graph is exported to `docs/design/reflow2.json`, and that file is committed. So a teammate without reflow2 can read it, and "what did the plan say in March" is answerable by `git log -p` on that one file plus the export's own `prev_content_hash` chain. The earlier objection — that graph-only breaks `req:design-reachable-without-the-repo` — does not hold: the information is reachable, it is merely not pretty, and prettiness is what on-demand rendering is for.

WHERE GIT KEEPS A REAL JOB, narrowed to where the thing being pinned actually lives in git: an ARRIVED epoch corresponds to real commits in real repos, and "what was actually deployed at epoch 3" is a question about the product, not the plan. That pin is a version combination (`req:version-combination-is-an-object`), and it is the backward direction only. Forward-looking plans describe graph content and stay in the graph; backward-looking arrivals describe code and pin code.

The in-repo precedent still holds and still shows the division: `rel:v0180` lives in the graph, tag `v0.18.0` lives in git, and nobody greps tags to learn what shipped.
